concepts.name: Agricultural Foundation and Land Revenue System
key_dimensions: Types of taxes levied on agricultural produce and their local names (e.g., siddaya, kattukattu)
Role of the nayankara system in agricultural administration and revenue extraction
Distinction between wet (irrigated) and dry land taxation rates
How revenue system compared to contemporaneous Mughal land revenue (zabti vs. Vijayanagara methods)

concepts.name: Nayankara System: Structure and Economic Implications
key_dimensions: Definition of amaram (military grant) held by nayakas and its revenue-sharing obligations to the central crown
Distinction between nayankara (military service grant) and the later fragmentation into semi-autonomous chieftains
Economic duties of nayakas: maintaining troops, remitting tribute, and local administration
UPSC trap: Difference between nayaka as an administrative officer vs. nayaka as a regional ruler in later period

concepts.name: Ayagar System and Village Economy
key_dimensions: Composition of the ayagar system: twelve hereditary village functionaries and their specific economic roles
Payment of ayagars in land grants (manyam) rather than cash — implications for a non-monetized village economy
Continuity of the ayagar system from earlier South Indian polities and its persistence into colonial period
UPSC trap: Distinguishing ayagar (South Indian) from the village panchayat structure described by Megasthenes or in North India

concepts.name: Vijayanagara's Overseas Trade: Commodities and Routes
key_dimensions: Key export commodities: cotton textiles, spices (pepper, cardamom), iron and steel, precious stones from Golconda mines
Key import commodities: Arabian horses (critical for military), elephants, copper, mercury, coral, and bullion
Major trade routes: western ports (Calicut, Cannanore, Bhatkal, Mangalore) and eastern ports (Masulipatnam, Pulicat)
Role of the Indian Ocean trade network connecting Vijayanagara to Persia, Arabia, China, and Southeast Asia

concepts.name: Horse Trade and its Strategic-Economic Significance
key_dimensions: Dependence on imported horses from Arabia and Persia due to inability to breed quality warhorses in South India
Role of Portuguese, Arab, and Persian merchants (particularly the Mappila traders) as horse suppliers
Economic leverage: how horse traders could influence Vijayanagara's military capacity and diplomatic relations
UPSC trap: Domingo Paes and Fernão Nunes (Portuguese chroniclers) as primary sources for horse trade — not to be confused with Abdur Razzaq (Central Asian)

concepts.name: Portuguese Presence and its Impact on Vijayanagara Trade
key_dimensions: Alliance between Vijayanagara and the Portuguese against common enemies (Bahmani/Deccan Sultans and Arab traders)
Portuguese control over Goa (1510) and its effect on redirecting horse and spice trade
Vijayanagara's policy of granting trading privileges to Portuguese in exchange for horses and firearms
Shift in trade dynamics: how Portuguese disrupted Arab and Mappila merchant dominance on the Malabar coast

concepts.name: Role of Merchant Guilds: Ayyavole and Manigramam
key_dimensions: Historical continuity of merchant guilds from early medieval period into Vijayanagara era
Ayyavole (Five Hundred Lords of Ayyavole/Aihole) as a long-distance trading corporation with pan-subcontinental reach
Distinction between Ayyavole (broader, inter-regional) and Manigramam (more localized, coastal trade focus)
UPSC trap: These guilds predate Vijayanagara — examiner may test whether candidates know their origin vs. their role under Vijayanagara

concepts.name: Textile Industry and Craft Production
key_dimensions: Vijayanagara as a major center for cotton and silk textile production destined for both domestic use and export
Organization of weavers into castes/guilds (e.g., Devangas, Kaikolas) with hereditary occupational rights
State patronage of craft production: royal workshops (karyashalas) versus independent artisan production
Role of textiles in diplomatic gift exchange and temple endowments — linking economy to polity and religion

concepts.name: Monetary System and Coinage
key_dimensions: Gold coins (varaha/hon/pagoda) as the primary currency — significance of gold availability from Karnataka mines
Silver and copper coins (fanam, kasu) for lower-denomination transactions in local markets
UPSC trap: 'Pagoda' — the gold coin of Vijayanagara — is frequently confused with the architectural term; examiner may test this dual meaning
Evidence of a monetized economy from inscriptions recording cash transactions in temples and markets

concepts.name: Markets, Bazaars, and Urban Commercial Centers
key_dimensions: Description of Hampi/Vijayanagara city's markets by foreign travelers (Abdur Razzaq, Paes, Barbosa) — evidence of vibrant commercial activity
Specialized markets: separate bazaars for cloth, precious stones, horses, and grain within the capital
Role of the 'bazaar street' (santha) connected to temples as a commercial-religious nexus
Comparison with contemporaneous market descriptions in Mughal cities — spatial organization and state regulation

concepts.name: Temple Economy and its Role in Trade Networks
key_dimensions: Temples as economic institutions: landholding, moneylending, warehousing, and employment generation
Temple endowments (danadharma) channeling merchant surplus into religious infrastructure
Role of temple towns (e.g., Tirupati, Srirangam) as nodes in regional and long-distance trade networks
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Vijayanagara temple economy from earlier Chola temple economy — continuity vs. change

concepts.name: Irrigation Infrastructure and its Economic Impact
key_dimensions: Construction of large-scale tanks and canals (e.g., Tungabhadra canal system) as state-sponsored agricultural investment
Krishna Deva Raya's inscriptions recording tank construction — linking royal piety to agrarian productivity
Economic multiplier effect: irrigation enabling double-cropping and supporting dense population in the Deccan
Comparison of Vijayanagara hydraulic infrastructure with Chola and later Mughal irrigation systems

concepts.name: Foreign Traveler Accounts as Economic Sources
key_dimensions: Abdur Razzaq (1443, Timurid ambassador): description of Calicut port and Vijayanagara city prosperity under Deva Raya II
Domingo Paes (c.1520, Portuguese): detailed account of markets, festivals, and Krishna Deva Raya's court wealth
Fernão Nunes (c.1535, Portuguese): focus on revenue, military expenditure, and trade under later rulers
UPSC trap: Matching the correct traveler to the correct ruler/period — Abdur Razzaq ≠ Krishna Deva Raya's era; Paes and Nunes = Krishna Deva Raya era

concepts.name: Role of the State in Trade Regulation and Taxation
key_dimensions: Levy of transit duties (sunkam/sunka) on goods passing through checkpoints — evidence of a regulated trade corridor system
State monopolies or preferential control over strategic commodities (elephants, horses, precious stones)
Role of the royal treasury (bhandara) in accumulating bullion from trade taxes — evidence for Krishnadeva Raya's legendary wealth
Distinction between central state taxation and nayaka-level taxation — potential for double taxation and its effect on traders

concepts.name: Spice Trade and Vijayanagara's Position in the Global Spice Network
key_dimensions: Vijayanagara's hinterland as a major source of pepper, cardamom, and other spices reaching the Malabar ports
Competition between Arab, Chinese, and later Portuguese merchants for control of the spice trade at Malabar ports
How spice trade revenues contributed to Vijayanagara's fiscal strength and ability to finance military campaigns
Connection between spice trade and European Age of Exploration — Vijayanagara as a key node in the global commodity chain

concepts.name: Mining Economy: Gold, Iron, and Precious Stones
key_dimensions: Karnataka's gold mines (Kolar gold fields) as a primary source of Vijayanagara's monetary gold and export commodity
Iron ore and steel production in the Deccan — export of high-quality Indian steel (wootz steel) to Persia and Arabia
Diamond mines of Golconda (nominally under Bahmani/later Qutb Shahi but traded through Vijayanagara networks)
UPSC trap: Golconda diamonds — political control (Bahmani/Deccan Sultanates) vs. trade networks (routed through Vijayanagara ports)

concepts.name: Caste, Occupational Guilds, and Economic Stratification
key_dimensions: Left-hand (idangai) vs. right-hand (valangai) caste factions and their disputes over trade route rights and market precedence
Economic privileges encoded in caste: specific castes monopolizing specific trades (e.g., Komati merchants for long-distance trade)
State arbitration of caste-trade disputes as a mechanism of economic governance
UPSC trap: Left-hand/right-hand factions are a South Indian phenomenon — not to be confused with North Indian jati hierarchies in trade

concepts.name: Decline of Vijayanagara Economy Post-Talikota (1565)
key_dimensions: Immediate economic impact: looting and destruction of Hampi disrupting the capital's commercial infrastructure
Long-term fragmentation: nayakas becoming independent rulers, redirecting trade revenues away from a central treasury
Shift of trade routes: decline of western Deccan ports and rise of Coromandel coast ports under successor nayaka kingdoms
UPSC trap: Talikota (1565) did not immediately end Vijayanagara — the empire survived in weakened form; economic decline was gradual, not instantaneous

concepts.name: Inter-regional Trade within the Subcontinent
key_dimensions: Trade links between Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates despite political rivalry — economic pragmatism over political hostility
Flow of goods between Vijayanagara and the Coromandel coast hinterland (textiles north; rice and cotton south)
Role of river systems (Krishna, Tungabhadra, Kaveri) as internal trade arteries
Comparison with Mughal internal trade networks — imperial road system (Mughal) vs. river/port-based networks (Vijayanagara)
